c11_soc_ch04.title: Culture and Socialisation
c11_soc_ch04.def: Culture in sociology is the shared, learned system of meanings, symbols, values, norms, and material artifacts that members of a society use to interpret their world and guide their behaviour, transmitted across generations through social interaction rather than biological inheritance.
c11_soc_ch04.mis: Students conflate 'culture' with 'high culture' (classical music, fine art) or 'tradition' (unchanging customs). c11_soc_ch04.dq: State Tylor's 1871 definition of culture verbatim as given in the NCERT text, and identify which two elements in his list are explicitly non-material.

c11_soc_ch05.title: Doing Sociology: Research Methods
c11_soc_ch05.def: The scientific method in sociology refers to the systematic, documented, and reflexive procedures through which sociological knowledge is produced, distinguishing it from common sense. Methodology is the philosophical study of these methods — their assumptions, limitations, and justification — while a method is a specific research technique (e.g., survey, participant observation, interview) used to gather data.
c11_soc_ch05.mis: Students conflate "methodology" with "method" — they think methodology is just a fancy word for the research technique used. c11_soc_ch05.dq: Define "methodology" and "method" in sociology. Give one example of each.

c11_soc_ch06.title: Social Structure, Stratification and Social Processes in Society
c11_soc_ch06.def: Social structure is the patterned, relatively stable arrangement of social institutions, statuses, roles, and norms that organises human interaction into predictable regularities across time and space, constraining and enabling individual action while being reproduced and transformed through that very action.

c11_soc_ch07.title: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Contexts
c11_soc_ch07.def: Social change refers to significant alterations in the underlying structure of society—including its institutions, norms, values, and social relationships—that are both intensive (transforming fundamentals) and extensive (affecting a large section of society), occurring over a measurable period of time. c11_soc_ch07.mis: Students equate 'social change' with any visible alteration in daily life—new gadgets, fashion, slang, or a single law—because these are salient and recent. c11_soc_ch08.title: Environment and Society
c11_soc_ch08.def: Ecology is the web of physical and biological systems and processes — including mountains, rivers, plains, oceans, flora, and fauna — of which humans are one element, shaped by the interaction between geography and hydrology, and modified over time by human action.
c11_soc_ch08.mis: Students treat "ecology" and "environment" as synonyms for "nature untouched by humans." They imagine a pristine wilderness that society then "impacts." c11_soc_ch09.def: The Enlightenment (late 17th–18th century), French Revolution (1789), and Industrial Revolution (late 18th–early 19th century) constitute the three foundational historical processes that transformed European society from feudal, religiously-dominated, agrarian orders into modern, secular, industrial nation-states, thereby creating the intellectual and material conditions that necessitated the emergence of sociology a

They
c11_soc_ch09.dq: Name the three revolutions identified in the NCERT text as creating the context for sociology's emergence, and state the century in which sociology was born.

c11_soc_ch10.title: Indian Sociologists
c11_soc_ch10.def: The institutional history of sociology in India refers to the formal establishment and development of university departments, research centres, and professional associations that transformed sociology from an amateur pursuit into an academic discipline, beginning with the University of Bombay's Department of Sociology in 1919 under G.S. c11_soc_ch10.dq: In which year and at which university was the first formal postgraduate department of sociology established in India, and who was its founding head?

c11_stat_ch01.title: Introduction to Statistics
c11_stat_ch01.def: Statistics in the **plural sense** refers to numerical data or quantitative facts systematically collected for a predetermined purpose (e.g., "Statistics show India's GDP grew by 7.2%"). Statistics in the **singular sense** refers to the scientific discipline comprising methods for collecting, organising, presenting, analysing, and interpreting numerical data to make informed decisions.

c11_stat_ch02.def: Primary data refers to original data collected first-hand by the investigator for a specific research purpose through direct methods such as surveys, experiments, or observations. Secondary data refers to data that has already been collected, processed, and published by other agencies (government, research institutions, organisations) for their own purposes and is being reused by the current investigator.
c11_stat_ch02.mis: **The "Hierarchy Bias" Misconception:** Students believe primary data is inherently "better," "more accurate," or "more scientific" than secondary data, and that secondary data is merely a fallback when primary collection is impossible. c11_stat_ch03.title: Organisation of Data
c11_stat_ch03.def: Classification of data is the systematic process of arranging raw, unorganised observations into homogeneous groups or classes based on shared characteristics or criteria, thereby transforming disorganised raw data into a structured format that facilitates comparison, analysis, and meaningful interpretation.
c11_stat_ch03.mis: Students believe that 'classification' and 'frequency distribution' are synonymous—they think constructing a frequency table with tally marks IS classification. c11_stat_ch04.def: Textual presentation of data is a method of describing statistical information entirely through written sentences or paragraphs, where numerical facts are embedded in narrative form. It is most suitable when the volume of data is small, allowing the presenter to emphasize specific observations or contextual nuances that might be lost in tabular or diagrammatic formats.

c11_stat_ch05.title: Measures of Central Tendency
c11_stat_ch05.def: An average (or measure of central tendency) is a single representative value that summarises an entire data set by identifying the central position around which all observations tend to cluster, enabling meaningful comparison and analysis of large volumes of data.

c11_stat_ch06.def: Measures of dispersion quantify the extent to which individual data points in a distribution deviate from a central value (mean, median, or mode), describing the spread, variability, or scatter of the dataset around its average.

c11_stat_ch07.def: Correlation is a statistical measure that quantifies the direction and strength of the linear relationship between two variables, indicating how they tend to change together without implying that one causes the other.

c11_stat_ch08.def: An index number is a statistical measure designed to show the average relative change in a group of related variables (such as prices, quantities, or values) between two time periods or across different situations, expressed as a percentage relative to a base period assigned the value 100.
